title.rendered: Why do we use a ‘fingers crossed’ approach to treating advanced cancer?

caption.rendered: I remember first hearing about genomics testing for cancer, about a year after my diagnosis of secondary breast cancer. I had failed on every line of treatment I’d been given, was fast running out of options and looking for a lifeline

alt_text: Why do we use a ‘fingers crossed’ approach to treating advanced cancer?

caption.rendered: It’s not always easy to accept help and support. I was diagnosed with cancer in my early thirties when I was already struggling with a lot of feelings of failure.
It’s not always easy to accept help and support. I was diagnosed with cancer in my early thirties when I was already struggling with a lot of feelings of failure.

METUPUK will advocate with life science companies to increase the number of MBC trials to a level reflective of the proportion of MBC patients within the breast cancer population. Trials offer real potential to save and extend lives. We want this to be recognised and participation encouraged.

title.rendered: Drugs, drugs, drugs, like patching up a sinking boat

caption.rendered: I think sometimes when those outside the cancer world imagine what treatment is like they think we go in, have some chemo, take some photos dancing round our IV pole and then go home and rest for a few days…. And don’t get me wrong I’m one of those people who have taken a cheeky chemo selfie and donned numerous items of leopard print to get me through those loooooooong days in the chemo ward, its like an armour for what is essentially a ritual poisoning!

alt_text: Drugs, drugs, drugs, like patching up a sinking boat

caption.rendered: I began taking Palbociclib over 3 years ago, badgering my Oncologist and accessing it through a free trial set up by Pfizer. The trial was designed to sway NICE into approving the drug for NHS use, despite it’s high price.
